title: Advice on Codex Game Design
author: AIDevJosh
selftext:
For those that primarily use Codex to build games, what model do you use, with what reasoning level? 

While I use Sonnet 5.5 (and like the output a lot), I want to use Codex more, as I have a x5 plan there currently, and can't fund a x5 plan with Claude at the moment. 

I just don't know how to properly implement bug fixes, etc, when it comes to the graphical side with Astra.

comments.author: Western-Hotel8723
comments.body: You need to learn how the systems actually work so you can tell it how to fix it.

replies.author: AIDevJosh
replies.body: Is it just by being specific on the issue that needs fixed?

replies.author: Western-Hotel8723
replies.body: You need to understand how the underlying system is broken. If ai doesn't know and you don't, then neither of you know lol.

replies.author: AIDevJosh
replies.body: I mean, visually I can tell when an issue has arisen, often is the case for a functional error as well, it's just wording it into the correct prompt that can be a struggle for me.

replies.author: Western-Hotel8723
replies.body:
Yes because you don't understand why it's broken.

AI is extremely powerful if you even understand the underlying system just a little. 

You need to work with it. It's not an AGI. It still needs help. Treat it like that.

replies.author: AIDevJosh
replies.body: Thanks. I think I understand what you mean.

replies.author: DancinFool82
replies.body: It does a really amazing job if you're well versed in programming and architecture. It's incredibly powerful, but it's worth spending some time learning how the systems should be structured and how to code

replies.author: redditscraperbot2
replies.body:
For example. I had an issue where typed dialogue choices were conflicting and being lost due to typos. I can point at the dialogue subsystem and tell the AI to change the typed flags into gameplay tags.

Really simple example and the AI probably could find that for you by just saying "I make lots of spelling mistakes and want you to fix it" but understanding how information is passed around your project makes it a lot easier to specify how you want things fixed.

comments.author: dilberry
comments.body: Use both - Claude for graphical design and Codex for generating assets, code, programming things like npc behaviors, anything involving images like menu icons, UI, item skins, textures, music/sounds, etc.

comments.author: LudwigLoewenlunte
comments.body:
Hi,

I've developed my game [Azzog's Idle Asteroid](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5325230/Azzogs_Idle_Asteroid/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=comment&utm_content=r_aigamedev) with Codex/Astra on low only.

I stumbled several times over gamebreaking bugs. For instance, Azzog can get stacked buffs from stuff, so it can happen that he breaks an ore and it breaks up into hundreds of smaller parts, that get physic sim.

The performance was getting to one digit FPS. But doing gamebreaking builds is most of the fun, so this needed to be fixed. I stated the situation for codex where the issue occurs, what issue I specifically experiences and what the state/definition of done should be.

It did performance fixes, so that now several thousand ore pieces can be on you asteroid.

For visual/graphical issues, I do the same approach. I screenshot the issue, I describe the wrong state that I am seeing. Than I describe the state I want the graphics to be in.

Just Imagine writing a JIRA Ticket for Sheldon Cooper

comments.author: AlgaeNo3373
comments.body:
Visual bugs can be a PITA because its way of understanding them can be limited to screenshots/code and not seeing the issue properly because of that. If you have something annoyingly persistent, you can have it help you write up an excrutiatingly detailed bug report with full repro steps etc - basically ask it to drill you with questions.  This will help you help it identify the core issue. 

That said if you're not already allowing screenshots/iterations into the workflow that's a great pre-emptive way to hammer out visual bugs before they materialize (GPT does a lot of visual iteration ime). 

I use Claude too, but lots of Astra/Sol 6.1 - light for stuff I'm doing hands-on, Ultra for unattended/overnight runs.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
I'm currently using Astra on Medium as an orchestrator which then creates 6.1 Sol High threads for each task. These agents then have authority to create sub agents if they want, though I don't monitor those too closely.

If you are on the Plus plan I don't think this will work for you. Kick your Orchestrator down to 6.1 Sol Medium. What will make a huge difference is getting your work organised so that each agent is only working with the context it needs.

* Get yourself a task manager and ask your orchestrator to manage it. Create tasks and handle them one at a time. This way you can stop scope creep and make the AI work logically
* Keep the scope of each task small
* Use the annotation tool in Codex to flag precisely where the issues are. Be clear in what is wrong and what you want instead. Letting the AI guess can keep the loop going for ever
* Provide external references to good examples of what you want and annotate these as well
* Make sure you have the final say on if something is finished. You own the final play test. Be thorough, the AI doesn't have an ego and doesn't get bored so you can really hammer it with detail

comments.author: lemonlemons
comments.body: Astra is the only model good enough for 3D in my opinion. I use Astra High and Extra High and get good results. Though the usage will go fast.
